stories.headline: Rep. Joe Neguse elected assistant House speaker for next Congress
stories.summary:
U.S. Rep. Joe Neguse, D-Colo., won election Wednesday as assistant speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives for the next Congress. The Lafayette Democrat was elected unanimously by his party and will be the fourth-highest-ranking member of the chamber's leadership.

Neguse recently played a visible role in Colorado Democratic events following the 2026 midterms. He gave welcoming remarks on Nov. 13 at the "What's Next" post-election Democratic Party gathering at The Mission Ballroom in Denver. He also spoke at the Colorado Democrats' election night watch party at the same venue.

The new leadership post elevates a member of Colorado's congressional delegation within House Democrats. Fox31 reported on Neguse's priorities in the role as the new Congress prepares to convene.

stories.headline: Two teens charged as adults with first-degree murder in June Denver shooting
stories.summary:
The Denver District Attorney's Office announced Wednesday that two teenagers have been charged with first-degree murder and attempted aggravated robbery. Jonathon Duron-Villanueva, 17, and Romell Escobedo, 16, are accused of shooting and killing 19-year-old Jacob Lopez on June 24.

Both defendants were charged as adults, District Attorney John Walsh said in a news release. The charges include allegations of an attempted aggravated robbery connected to the killing.

The case will proceed through Denver's criminal courts. The defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

stories.headline: Group plans 2027 Colorado bill to raise penalties for underage vape sales
stories.summary:
The Rocky Mountain Smoke-Free Alliance announced Wednesday that it will push legislation in the 2027 Colorado session to increase penalties for selling vaping products to minors. The nonprofit trade association represents the state's independent vape retailers and manufacturers of alternative nicotine products.

The proposed Colorado Youth Nicotine Prevention and Accountability Act would explore using existing nicotine tax revenue for enforcement. It would restrict products designed to appeal to children, such as devices with video games or items disguised as school supplies, and require online retailers to use age-verification technology. It would also add products such as nicotine pouches, e-cigarettes, lozenges and gum to the Colorado Certified Brands Directory.

Spokesperson John Paul Willett, an Arizona-based vape retailer who also owns Colorado stores, said the group has at least one legislative sponsor. He helped shape a similar Arizona law signed June 4. Denver voters upheld a flavored tobacco sales ban in November 2025, and opponents say it will cost the city more than $13 million in lost tax revenue.

stories.headline: Waymo to expand across metro Denver as self-driving trucks arrive
stories.summary:
Denver drivers will soon see more self-driving vehicles, officials said Wednesday. Waymo, the most prominent autonomous operator in the city, plans to expand its passenger service to all of metro Denver and Denver International Airport in the coming months.

Autonomous trucks and other self-driving vehicles are also expected to enter the market. The expansion comes despite some friction on the roads between autonomous vehicles and other traffic.

During the Wednesday meeting, Denver Police Lt. Michael Wyatt said the department has found some workarounds in dealing with the vehicles, including in situations involving tickets.

stories.headline: Federal judge holds ICE in contempt over re-detentions in Colorado
stories.summary:
A Colorado federal judge on Wednesday held Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials in contempt of court for repeatedly violating judicial orders. The violations involved re-detaining immigrants after courts had ordered them released from detention.

The judge ruled that officials were in clear contempt of a federal court's order when they rearrested a recently released immigrant detainee in Aurora last month. The judge said ICE had made a mockery of court orders in Colorado.

The ruling adds judicial scrutiny to immigration enforcement in the Denver area, where Aurora hosts a major detention facility.

stories.headline: Denver weighs $822,000 in raises for 12 of mayor's top appointees
stories.summary:
Denver is considering $822,000 in pay raises for 12 of Mayor Mike Johnston's top appointees, ranging from 10% to 60%. The proposal also includes a mechanism for automatic raises in the future. Of the estimated $822,346 in added annual costs, $572,010 would come from the General Fund.

Councilmember Amanda Sawyer, in her final term, proposed the ordinance. It would raise salaries Jan. 1 and set automatic adjustments every four years beginning in 2031 without further council approval. Sawyer said the raises would correct pay disparities in which some department heads earn less than employees they supervise.

The proposal comes less than two weeks after the city approved a $1.68 billion General Fund budget for 2027, a 1.1% increase. City departments have been asked to rein in spending after a year of layoffs and a freeze on merit raises for career service employees. In May 2025, Johnston postponed a similar proposal of up to 44% raises after council concerns. Sawyer acknowledged the optics but said Denver must stay competitive.

stories.headline: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth; CU scientist has followed the mission
stories.summary:
Nearly 50 years after its launch, Voyager 1 has reached another historic milestone: it is now one light-day from Earth.

Fran Bagenal, a scientist at the University of Colorado's Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics, has been along for the ride for most of that time. She has worked with data from Voyager 1 since her days as a graduate student.

The milestone underscores the long-running contributions of Colorado researchers to space science, as the spacecraft continues to travel through interstellar space.

stories.headline: Colorado Springs project plans 40 affordable teacher homes on school grounds
stories.summary:
Harrison School District 2 and the nonprofit We Fortify broke ground Nov. 12 on Wendy's Village, a development of 40 compact homes for educators on an acre of Mountain Vista Community School grounds in Colorado Springs. Rents are planned below $1,000 a month, though exact figures have not been set. The project still required some environmental clearances.

The 352-square-foot one-bedroom homes will be built as 20 duplexes, some modular and some built on site by Colarelli Construction. Plans include electric heating, air conditioning, washers and dryers, garden beds and a community center. Homes are intended for early-career teachers below an income limit; a first-year Harrison teacher with a bachelor's degree starts at $50,500. Leases can be renewed for up to three years.

The fundraising target has grown from $6.2 million to $10.5 million, including $1 million in congressional spending arranged by Sens. John Hickenlooper and Michael Bennet. A district survey found interest at four times capacity.

stories.headline: Murray's late shot and free throw lift Nuggets past Celtics 105-101
stories.summary:
The Denver Nuggets beat the Boston Celtics 105-101 on Wednesday to improve to 8-5. Denver had entered play at 7-5, with inconsistent results early in the season.

Jamal Murray hit a midrange shot with about seven seconds left to put Denver up 104-101. He then made a free throw after Jayson Tatum was called for a technical foul. Murray finished with 21 points, seven rebounds, two assists, four steals and two blocks, and defended well against Boston's guards, including Payton Pritchard.

Coach David Adelman praised him afterward, calling him a two-way player, an All-Star and a clutch performer who can adapt to what the team needs on a given night.

stories.headline: U.S. outdoor recreation economy hits record $1.3 trillion; Colorado ranks 10th
stories.summary:
The U.S. outdoor recreation economy topped $1.3 trillion in 2025, according to Bureau of Economic Analysis figures released Wednesday. Growth slowed to 1.9% over 2024, below the 2.3% growth of the national economy and down from 2.5% the prior year. The sector accounts for 2.3% of the U.S. economy and supports 5.3 million jobs.

Colorado's outdoor recreation economy ranked 10th nationally, with $18.5 billion in activity supporting 137,415 jobs. That is up $400 million from 2024, about half the growth measured between 2023 and 2024. Outdoor-related manufacturing contributed $987 million, down from $1.1 billion, and shops selling outdoor goods delivered a $3.6 billion impact, down from $3.7 billion.

Colorado ranks first for winter activities, with $1.75 billion in economic activity, more than double California's. The Outdoor Recreation Roundtable called for passage of the America the Beautiful Act, which would reauthorize public lands spending.

stories.headline: Aerospace firm Leap signs first lease at Broomfield's Arista 36 industrial site
stories.summary:
Aerospace company Leap has leased 75,000 square feet at Broomfield's Arista 36 industrial site, the park's first lease. The space will house the company's headquarters.

The lease will also allow Leap to expand production through 2027, according to the Denver Business Journal.

The deal gives the Broomfield industrial development an anchor tenant in Colorado's aerospace sector.

stories.headline: Eight of 12 counties back Front Range Passenger Rail District tax
stories.summary:
Eight of the 12 counties within the Front Range Passenger Rail District's funding area voted yes on a new tax to fund the Colorado Connector line, according to results of the November election.

The tax is intended to support the passenger rail project along the Front Range. Results varied by county across the district's funding area.

Coloradoan published a county-by-county breakdown of how voters in the district's area voted.

topStory.headline: Putin Warns Russia Will Respond to Strikes on Crimean Bridge After Trilateral Talks With Trump and Xi
topStory.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Russia "will respond to strikes on the Crimean Bridge" during a press briefing following a trilateral meeting among Russia, China and the United States. The remarks, reported by the Russian state news agency RIA Novosti and carried in The Guardian's live coverage, came after what the news topic described as unprecedented talks among the three leaders, with the war in Ukraine and nuclear arms on the agenda.

Putin spoke warmly of U.S. President Donald Trump, saying he has "no doubts" that Trump "sincerely strives both for the resolution of conflicts, including the Ukrainian one, and sincerely strives to improve bilateral relations across a whole range of areas." Putin added that improving ties on the U.S.-Russian track was, in his words, important for Moscow. The source material does not detail what Chinese President Xi Jinping said at the briefing or what Trump said about the talks.

Putin also criticized Kyiv and European capitals, claiming that Ukraine's leadership was stalling peace efforts. This is consistent with Moscow's long-standing position that responsibility for the lack of a settlement lies with Ukraine and its European backers. The Crimean Bridge, linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula it annexed from Ukraine in 2014, has been a repeated target of attacks during the war, and Russia has previously carried out retaliatory strikes after such incidents.

The meeting brings together the leaders of the three largest nuclear-armed powers at a time of unresolved fighting in Ukraine and uncertainty over the future of strategic arms control. Putin's warning over the bridge signals that Moscow is maintaining a firm stance on military escalation even as it speaks positively of diplomacy with Washington. Further details on any agreements, joint statements or follow-up negotiations had not been confirmed in the available reporting, and developments are expected as the leaders and their governments provide additional accounts of the talks.
